# **Amazon SageMaker \- Overview**

Now let's talk about **Amazon SageMaker**, which is one of the most important **machine learning services** on AWS. It's a **fully managed service** for developers and data scientists who want to **build machine learning models** and also **deploy them**. Typically, doing all the processes in one place around machine learning is very difficult. On top of that, when you start training models, you need to have **compute resources** or servers, and provisioning them is also difficult. **SageMaker does it all for you in one place**.

## **How SageMaker Works \- Example**

For example, say you want to build a model to predict your next exam score for your AWS exam. Here's how that works:

![][image1]

* We start with **historical data** (see the diagram above) and transform it (Feature Engineering) to extract:

  * Number of years of experience in IT  
  * Number of years of experience with AWS  
  * How long the student has spent on this course  
  * Their passing score (this is the output)  
* We know this because this is **historical data** that we have collected over time  
* For example, if I did a survey to my students asking all these questions as well as their exam score, they would say 670, 890, and 934

Once we have all these datasets with as many rows as possible, we **build our machine learning model** directly on SageMaker. It helps us **train and tune our model**. 

Then, when the model is built and you as a new student who hasn't passed the exam yet say "Hey, I have three years of experience in IT, one year of experience on AWS, and have spent 10 hours on this course," → the model will apply to the data and say the **prediction** is that you will pass the exam with a 906 score.

## **SageMaker Core Functions**

All of these things can happen directly on SageMaker. To summarize, SageMaker helps you:

1. **Collect and prepare data**  
2. **Build and train machine learning models**  
3. **Deploy the models**  
4. **Monitor the performance** of the predictions and models to go back to the first stage and improve data collection

   ![][image2]

## **SageMaker – Built-in Algorithms**

If you want to go a little deeper, there are some **built-in algorithms** on SageMaker. You don't need to know them, but here's what SageMaker can do:

### **Supervised Algorithms**

* **Linear regressions** and **classifications**  
* Classification using **KNN algorithms**

  ### **Unsupervised Algorithms**

* **PCA (Principal Component Analysis)** \- to reduce the number of features in the dataset  
* **K-means** \- to find grouping within the data  
* **Anomaly detection** \- to find datasets or data points that look different (could be used for **fraud**)

  ### **Additional Capabilities**

* **Machine learning on text** \- **NLP (natural language processing)** or **summarization**  
* **Image processing** \- such as **classification** and **detection** (like object detection)

You do not need to remember these things, but SageMaker has many more built-in algorithms and is a **one-stop place** to do your machine learning.

| Linear regression \- Predicts a number based on input data, like predicting house price from size and location. Classification \- Sorts things into categories, like determining if an email is spam or not spam. KNN algorithms \- Looks at the closest similar examples to make a decision, like "if 3 nearby houses sold for $300k, yours is probably around $300k too." PCA \- Removes unnecessary details from data to make it simpler, like reducing 100 features to 10 most important ones. K-means \- Groups similar data points together automatically, like separating customers into different buying behavior groups. Anomaly detection \- Finds unusual patterns that don't fit normal behavior, commonly used to catch fraudulent transactions. NLP \- Processes human language for tasks like translating text or creating summaries. Image processing \- Analyzes pictures to identify objects or classify what's in the image. |
| :---- |

## **Automatic Model Tuning (AMT)**

Something that's very cool about SageMaker is called **Automatic Model Tuning (AMT)**. The idea is that you have your model, but you want to make sure that you try different parameter combinations to **tune your model** and see if you can get better performance out of it. While this could be manual, in SageMaker it is **automatic**.

![][image3]

**How AMT Works:**

* We define the **objective metric** \- what do we want to optimize for?  
* AMT automatically chooses the **hyperparameter ranges**  
* It figures out a **search strategy** \- how to navigate the hyperparameter ranges  
* It determines **how long to run** the tuning job  
* It sets **early stop conditions** if a job is not tuning itself well

Bottom line: we just say "Hey, we want to optimize for this objective metric" and **SageMaker does the rest**. It **saves you lots of time and money**, and helps you not waste money on suboptimal configurations due to the **early stop condition**.

## **Sagemaker – Model Deployment & Inference**

Once you have trained your model, you need to **deploy it**. In SageMaker it's super easy \- you just **deploy it with one click** and automatically get:

* **Automatic scaling**  
* **No server management** (as opposed to a **self-hosted solution** where you would deploy your own models on your own servers)  
* Because we have a **managed solution** with SageMaker, there's a lot of **reduced overhead**.

| What is "overhead" in machine learning? Overhead refers to all the extra work, time, and resources you need to spend on infrastructure and management tasks instead of focusing on your actual machine learning work. "Reduced overhead" means: Instead of spending 60% of your time on infrastructure management and 40% on actual ML work, you can spend 90%+ of your time on building and improving your models. Real example: Without SageMaker: 2 weeks to set up infrastructure \+ 1 week to build model With SageMaker: 1 day to build model (infrastructure handled automatically) |
| :---- |

## **SageMaker Deployment Types**

### **1\. Real-time Inference (see the diagram below)**

* This is **One prediction at a time**  
* We’ll have **Real-time endpoint** where our application sends a payload  
* We configure the **CPU or GPU** for models to do **inference** (compute the outcome)  
* We will have **Auto scaling** included  
* So that we can get answer **right away**

**![][image4]**

### **2\. Serverless Inference**

* This is very **Similar architecture to real-time**  
* Over here we only select how much **memory** you want for your models (depending on what models do we have)  
* **Auto scaling done out of the box** \- **no configuration needed** (we don’t have to configure it) → (if you don’t understand Autoscaling, read it below after the diagram)  
* For serverless, we can have periods with **no traffic**  
  * **Downside:** **Cold start** \- if you start having traffic after no traffic for a long time, the model has to boot up first, causing more **latency** on the first call → (if you don’t understand Cold Start, read it below after the diagram)  
    

![][image5]

| More about Autoscaling for Real-time & Serverless Inference: Real-time Inference Autoscaling: Autoscaling is INCLUDED \- meaning it's available/provided by default You CAN configure it \- set minimum/maximum instances, scaling policies, etc. You have control over scaling parameters \- when to scale up/down, how many instances Example: You can set "minimum 2 instances, maximum 10 instances, scale up when CPU \> 70%" Serverless Inference Autoscaling: Autoscaling is "out of the box" \- meaning it's completely automatic and managed You CANNOT configure it \- AWS handles everything automatically Zero configuration needed \- AWS decides when and how to scale Example: AWS automatically handles everything \- you just use it, no settings to configure What does "out of the box" mean? "Out of the box" \= Ready to use immediately with no setup or configuration required Think of it like: Real-time \= Car with manual transmission (you control the gears/scaling) Serverless \= Car with automatic transmission (it handles everything for you) Key Difference: Real-time: Autoscaling available, but YOU configure it Serverless: Autoscaling happens automatically, NO configuration needed Both have autoscaling, but serverless removes the burden of configuring it. |
| :---- |

### 

| What is Latency? Latency \= The time it takes from when you send a request to when you get the response back. Example: You ask "What's 2+2?" and it takes 0.5 seconds to get "4" back → That's 0.5 seconds latency. What is Cold Start? Cold start happens when your serverless model has been "sleeping" (no traffic for a while) and needs to "wake up" first. In SageMaker Serverless: When model is "warm" (recently used): Request → Response in 100ms (low latency) When model is "cold" (hasn't been used for 15+ minutes): Request → Model boots up (5 seconds) → Then processes → Response in 5.1 seconds (high latency) After the first call: All subsequent calls are fast again (100ms) until it goes "cold" again Why does this happen? Serverless \= AWS turns off your model when not in use (to save money) When you need it again \= AWS has to start it up first |
| :---- |

### **3\. Asynchronous Inference**

* For **very large payloads** (up to **1 gigabyte**), it will have **Long processing time**  
* Therefore, we have to put the payload into **Staging Amazon S3 bucket**  
* Then the Application tells asynchronous endpoint to put job in **queue**  
* **The Computation happens in its own time**  
* Results go to another **Amazon S3 bucket**  
* This approach provides **Near real-time latency** \- meaning that you don't get answer right away, but you'll get it at some point

![][image6]

### **4\. Batch Transform**

* This is used for making **Prediction for entire dataset** \- (that is you want **multiple predictions**)  
* It has **Similar architecture to asynchronous**  
* The request and response is in **Amazon S3** (Look the diagram below)  
* So our application is put the Dataset in the staging bucket (Look the diagram below)  
* Then, the **Batch endpoint** puts job in **job queue**  
* And then the **Results** go to result **Amazon S3 bucket**

**![][image7]**

## **Deployment Types Comparison**

| Inference Type | Latency | Payload Size | Processing Time | Use Case |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Real-time Inference** | **Low** (milliseconds to seconds) | Up to **6 MB**, **1 record** | Max **60 seconds** | **Fast, near-instant predictions** for web/mobile apps |
| **Serverless Inference** | **Low** (with **cold start** caveat) | Up to **6 MB**, (**1 record**) | Max **60 seconds** | Sporadic, short-term inference **without infrastructure**, can tolerate **Cold Starts** |
| **Asynchronous Inference** | Medium to High (**Near Real time**) | Up to **1 GB**, (**1 record**) | Max **1 hour** | **Large payloads**, and workloads that require **longer processing times** |
| **Batch Transform** | **High** (minutes to hours) | Up to **100 MB** per invocation (per mini batch) | Max **1 hour** | **Bulk** **processing** for large datasets; **Concurrent processing.** Also if it requires to **Multiple Predictions** |

**Key Exam Keywords:**

* **No infrastructure** → **Serverless**  
* **Real-time** → **Real-time** or **Serverless** inference  
* **Near real-time** → **Asynchronous** inference  
* **Large payloads** → **Asynchronous** or **Batch**  
* **Multiple records** → **Batch Transform**

## **SageMaker Studio**

When you use the SageMaker service, you will most certainly use **SageMaker Studio**. This is the **interface** which allows you to do **end-to-end machine learning development** directly from **one specific place**.

![][image8]

**SageMaker Studio Features:**

* You have **Team collaboration** \- different teammates can work together  
* You can **Tune and debug** machine learning models  
* You can **Deploy** machine learning models  
* You can **Perform automated workflows**

**SageMaker Studio** will be at the **center** of what we do in SageMaker.

## **Summary**

We've seen a very high overview of SageMaker. We know that we can:

1. **Train the model** on SageMaker  
2. **Automatically tune the model** on SageMaker  
3. **Deploy the model** on SageMaker in **four different ways** (**real-time**, **serverless**, **asynchronous**, and **batch transform**)
